questions.q: What problem does Resource Governor exist to solve?
options: Without limits, SQL Server hands out CPU and memory to whatever asks for it, so one noisy workload can starve every other session sharing the same instance; Resource Governor caps how much a given workload can consume
It exists to encrypt data at rest for compliance purposes
It exists to automatically rebuild fragmented indexes
It exists to schedule SQL Server Agent jobs
questions.explain: Resource Governor's entire purpose is preventing one workload from consuming capacity that other sessions need, on the same instance.

questions.q: What are the three pieces of Resource Governor and how do they relate to each other?
options: A resource pool sets the actual CPU/memory ceiling; a workload group sits inside a pool and inherits its limits; a classifier function runs at login and decides which workload group a session joins
A login, a role, and a permission — the same three pieces used for authorization
A job, a step, and a schedule
A database, a table, and an index
questions.explain: Pool defines the ceiling, workload group is where a session lives day to day, and the classifier function routes sessions into groups at login.

questions.q: What happens if you configure a resource pool, workload group, and classifier function but forget to run ALTER RESOURCE GOVERNOR RECONFIGURE?
options: None of the configuration takes effect — Resource Governor changes are staged, not live, until RECONFIGURE is run
The configuration takes effect immediately regardless of RECONFIGURE
SQL Server automatically runs RECONFIGURE every hour
The classifier function is deleted automatically
questions.explain: RECONFIGURE is the step that actually applies staged Resource Governor changes.

questions.q: On which Azure SQL deployment options is Resource Governor actually available?
options: SQL Server on an Azure VM and Azure SQL Managed Instance — anywhere with instance-level control; it is not available on Azure SQL Database
Only on Azure SQL Database
On all three deployment options equally, with no platform difference
It is not available on any Azure SQL deployment option
questions.explain: Resource Governor requires instance-level access. Azure SQL Database handles the same problem differently, through its own service-tier resource limits.

questions.q: In the reporting-service-account example, how does capping that login's workload group at 30% CPU and 25% memory protect the OLTP workload?
options: The classifier function routes that login into a workload group whose resource pool physically cannot exceed those limits, so even the worst reporting query can't take capacity away from OLTP sessions
It automatically kills any OLTP query that runs too long
It moves the reporting workload to a completely separate physical server
It has no actual effect on resource consumption, only on logging
questions.explain: The pool's ceiling is enforced regardless of how demanding the reporting query is, which is what protects the rest of the instance's capacity.
